summary:
Still Out There is an interactive story map of NASA hardware. Since the 1960s NASA has left rovers, landers and probes on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Some still work, some finished their missions, and some have gone quiet. The project tells their stories so school-age space fans can meet the machines and the science they made possible.

Students see 17 machines on one distance map and pick a place to explore. Each machine shows its status, a short story, three facts to remember and a link to the open data behind it. A bonus tool shows how long a radio message to each machine takes. A live countdown follows Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026.

The facts come from public NASA pages and partner agency data from ISRO and ESA. The next step is to connect live NASA data, such as official photos and exact distances.
details:
Project details: Still Out There

What does it do and how does it work?
Still Out There is a website that puts 17 NASA machines on one distance map, from the Moon to interstellar space. A student picks a place (Moon, Mars, near the Sun, far out) or a status and taps a machine. The machine's page shows:

  • a status: still working, mission complete, or out of contact
  • a short story and the science it made possible
  • three facts to remember
  • a link to the open data behind it

A "How long would a hello take?" tool shows how long a radio message to each machine takes. A live countdown follows Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026. The site works on phones and in light or dark mode.

What are the benefits?

  • A student can answer one question quickly: is it still talking?
  • Each story is short and plain, so it works for school-age readers.
  • Every claim links to a public source, so students can check it.
  • The distance map and radio-delay tool make huge distances easier to grasp.

What impact is intended?
We want students to see space exploration as ongoing, with machines that outlive their plans and keep working. We also want them to learn that NASA's data is free to explore. A teacher could use it as a starting point for lessons on the solar system, light-speed delays and how science is checked.

What tools and software did we use?

  • HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript for the website, with no frameworks. The Voyager countdown and the radio-delay calculator are written in JavaScript.
  • Inline SVG for the machine drawings.
  • Google Fonts (Lexend, Unbounded, DM Mono).
  • Claude to research, write and build the site and the deck.
  • Headless Chrome (Playwright) to capture screenshots, and pptxgenjs to build the PowerPoint.

No special hardware was needed.

What data does it use?
NASA mission pages and news provided the dates and status. Partner data from ISRO (Chandrayaan images of Apollo sites and of India's Vikram lander) and ESA (Huygens, the ExoMars orbiter, Hera) appears in the stories. The prototype uses facts I curated from these sources. It does not call live NASA APIs yet. Connecting the NASA Image and Video Library, the Mars Rover Photos API and JPL Horizons is the planned next step.

How is it creative?

  • It organises the machines by whether they are still talking, which gives a story with a status instead of a plain list.
  • The log-scale map keeps the Moon and Voyager 1 on one screen.
  • The page follows a real event in progress: Voyager 1's light-day milestone.
  • The status uses colour and shape together, so it doesn't rely on colour alone.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy: I checked key facts against sources and marked Voyager 2 and the Pioneers as estimates. Hera's arrival is worded as "was due" because I found no confirmation that it had happened.
  • Audience: plain language, short text, readable type sizes.
  • Access: works on phones, in both themes, with keyboard focus and reduced-motion support.
  • Honesty: the page says which parts are live and which are planned.
  • Scope: 17 machines, which is enough to tell the story without overwhelming a student.
